title: Nanquan's cat
hookLine: a hard koan: monks quarrel over a cat; Zhaozhou puts his sandals on his head (Gateless Gate 14)
tomorrow: Every day is a good day
last: ORIGINAL FACE — BEFORE YOU WERE BORN.

cards: A quarrel, a cat, a sharp blade, and then, strangely, a pair of straw sandals worn as a hat. It's the fourteenth case of the Gateless Gate.
Every tradition has stories its own people argue about: stories that don't sit right, that get skipped in the nice version, that make a thoughtful reader put the book down for a minute.
Zen has several, and this is one of them. Fair warning: an animal dies in this story. i'll tell it plainly, say what Buddhists themselves say about it, and not pretend it's comfortable.

teach.b: At Nanquan's monastery, the monks of the eastern hall and the western hall were quarreling over a cat. Who it belonged to, the story doesn't say. Nanquan picked the cat up and held it out.

teach.h: SAY A TRUE WORD, OR THE CAT.
teach.b: He said: if any of you can say a true word, I'll spare the cat. If not, I'll cut it. No one could answer.
Nanquan cut the cat in two. That evening Zhaozhou, Nanquan's student, the one from mu and the washed bowl, came back from a trip. Nanquan told him what had happened.
Zhaozhou took off his straw sandals, put them on his head, and walked out. Nanquan said: if you had been there, the cat would have been saved. So what do Buddhists do with this?
The first precept is not to take life, and the story seems to break it. Teachers answer in different ways. Some say it probably never happened, a teaching story meant to shock, like Juzhi's finger.
Some say Nanquan took the harm on himself to cut through the monks' quarrel. Some modern teachers say plainly that the story troubles them and that no teaching justifies killing.
Those who keep the koan say it asks something real. The monks were so caught in owning and arguing that when life itself was on the line, they froze.
Zhaozhou's sandals on the head seem to say: you had it upside down.
The quarrel was on top and the cat was underfoot. Nobody has one agreed answer. That's why it's called hard.

how: Zen teachers present Nanquan's cat as a hard koan; some openly discuss the conflict between the story and the precept against taking life, and it is studied rather than held up as an example.

games.q: you're Zhaozhou. you come home in the evening and your teacher tells you what happened to the cat. what do you do, as the story tells it?
o: argue with him about the precept.
put your sandals on your head and walk out.
say nothing and go to bed.
games.why: Zhaozhou put his sandals on his head, and Nanquan said: if you'd been there, the cat would have been saved.

practice: Let this story, or another story that disturbs you, sit in the room with you, without rushing to fix it, excuse it or throw it out. Notice what it does in the body, a tight jaw, a turned stomach, and breathe with that.
You might ask quietly what a true word would have been; if no answer comes, let that be all right, since some stories are carried, not solved.
